'''Henry Bennion Eyring''' (born May 31, 1933) is an American religious leader and former educational administrator serving as the first counselor in the [[First Presidency (LDS Church)|First Presidency]] of [[the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints]] (LDS Church). As the church's second most senior [[Apostle (LDS Church)|apostle]],<ref>Apostolic seniority is generally understood to include all ordained apostles (including the [[First Presidency (LDS Church)|First Presidency]] and the [[Quorum of the Twelve Apostles (LDS Church)|Quorum of the Twelve Apostles]]. Seniority is determined by date of ordination, not by age or other factors. If two apostles are ordained on the same day, the older of the two is typically ordained first. See [[President of the Church (LDS Church)#Succession to the presidency|Succession to the presidency]] and {{cite journal |last= Heath |first= Steven H. |url=https://www.dialoguejournal.com/wp-content/uploads/sbi/articles/Dialogue_V20N02_46.pdf |title=Notes on Apostolic Succession |journal=Dialogue: A Journal of Mormon Thought |volume=20 |issue=2 |pages=44–56 |date=Summer 1987 }}.</ref> he is also the [[President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles (LDS Church)|President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles]], with [[Dieter F. Uchtdorf]] serving as the quorum's [[Acting President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles|acting president]]. 

Born in [[Princeton, New Jersey]], Eyring earned a [[bachelor's degree]] in [[physics]] from the [[University of Utah]] in 1955 and later received [[Master of Business Administration|MBA]] and [[Doctor of Business Administration|DBA]] degrees from [[Harvard University]]. He served two years in the [[United States Air Force|U.S. Air Force]] before beginning a career in academia. He was a professor of business at [[Stanford University]] from 1962 to 1971, also serving as a Sloan Visiting Fellow at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT). He was the president of Ricks College (now [[Brigham Young University–Idaho]]) from 1971 to 1977.

Eyring has been an LDS Church [[general authority]] since 1985. He was a counselor in the [[Presiding Bishop (LDS Church)|Presiding Bishopric]] from 1985 to 1992, then became a member of the [[First Quorum of the Seventy]] until he was [[Calling (LDS Church)|called]] to the [[Quorum of the Twelve Apostles (LDS Church)|Quorum of the Twelve Apostles]] in 1995. He served twice as [[Commissioner of Church Education|commissioner]] of the [[Church Educational System]], first from 1980 to 1985 and again from 1992 to 2005. 

==Early life==
Eyring was born on May 31, 1933, in Princeton, New Jersey, the second child of [[Henry Eyring (chemist)|Henry Eyring]], then a professor at Princeton and later the dean of the graduate school at the [[University of Utah]] and president of the [[American Chemical Society]], and his wife, Mildred Bennion. Eyring's aunt, Camilla Eyring, was the wife of [[Spencer W. Kimball]], the twelfth president of the LDS Church.

He lived in Princeton until his early teenage years. Until the start of [[World War II]], they attended LDS meetings at the branch in [[New Brunswick, New Jersey]], but with the gasoline rationing of the war, they received permission to hold meetings in their home, which often had only the Eyring family.<ref>{{citation |url= https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/ensign/2008/07/president-henry-b-eyring-called-of-god |author-link= Robert D. Hales |first= Robert D. |last= Hales |title= President Henry B. Eyring: Called of God |journal= [[Ensign (LDS magazine)|Ensign]] |date=July 2008 |page= 10 }}</ref> As a teenager, Eyring and his family moved to [[Salt Lake City]], where his father took a post at the [[University of Utah]].

==Military service and education==
Eyring spent two years in the U.S. Air Force, stationed at [[Sandia Base]] in New Mexico. In New Mexico, Eyring served as a [[district (LDS Church)|district]] missionary for the LDS Church.<ref>[https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/ensign/2013/05/we-are-one?lang=eng "We Are One"], ''Ensign'', May 2013.</ref> Eyring had been in the ROTC at the University of Utah. While in the Air Force, he served as a liaison between military officers and scientists. His main responsibility was to analyze data from weapons tests of nuclear weapons. At the end of the assignment, he gave a report and ended up meeting in person with a collection of several leading generals.<ref>Rober I. Eaton and Henry J. Eyring. ''I Will Lead You Along: The Life of Henry B. Eyring''. Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Company, 2013, p. 65-67</ref>

Eyring had previously received a bachelor's degree in physics from the University of Utah in 1955. He went on to earn both MBA and DBA degrees in business administration from the [[Harvard Business School]] before embarking on a career in academia. Over the summer after his first year at Harvard, Eyring did an internship with [[Arthur D. Little]] as a consultant for [[Abitibi Power and Paper Company]]. He did an analysis to study how to improve the process of river logging. His suggestion was to abandon river logging and turn to truck transport of logs, but a combination of not studying the issue deeply enough and having a CEO of the company who had risen through the ranks from being a river logger prevented Eyring's suggestions from being adopted then.<ref>Rober I. Eaton and Henry J. Eyring. ''I Will Lead You Along: The Life of Henry B. Eyring''. Salt Lake City: Deseret Book Company, 2013, p. 76-80</ref>

While studying at Harvard, Eyring was heavily influenced by [[Georges Doriot]], who offered Eyring a chance to work with him and [[Ken Olsen]], the founder of [[Digital Equipment Company]]. Eyring chose instead to pursue a doctorate in business.<ref>Eaton and Eyring, ''I Will Lead You Along'', p. 81-83</ref>

==Academic and business career==
In the fall of 1962, Eyring began work as a professor at Stanford University. He finished his doctorate in business in the summer of 1963.<ref>Eaton and Eyring, ''I Will Lead You Along'', p. 105</ref> That summer, Eyring completed a fellowship with the RAND Corporation.<ref>Eaton and Eyring, ''I Will Lead You Along'', p. 106</ref> Eyring had married his wife, Kathleen, the summer before he started at Stanford, and they spent their first year of married life moving through various homes his real estate developer father-in-law was in the process of refurbishing. They then spent the next ten years living in the guest house of his in-laws' property.<ref>Eaton and Eyring, ''I Will Lead You Along'', p. 108</ref>

Among Eyring's associates at Stanford were Roger Sant and [[Ed Zschau]]. Eyring worked with Zschau in the founding of the computer company System Industries.<ref>Eaton and Eyring, ''I Will Lead You Along'', p. 112</ref>

Eyring was an associate professor of business at the [[Stanford Graduate School of Business]] from 1962 to 1971.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/nation/5193935.html|newspaper=Houston Chronicle|title=President of Mormon Church appoints new adviser|first=Jennifer|last=Dobner|date=7 October 2007|agency=([[Associated Press|AP]])|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110521212758/http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/nation/5193935.html|archive-date=21 May 2011}}</ref> He was also a Sloan Visiting Faculty Fellow at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. At MIT, he took multiple courses in human behavior, including courses from [[Douglas McGregor]], who died of a heart attack while Eyring was at MIT, and also Ed Schein and [[Warren Bennis]].<ref>''I Will Lead You Along'', p. 113-115</ref>

Eyring has served twice as commissioner of church education, from September 1980 to April 1985, and from September 1992 to January 2005, when he was replaced by [[W. Rolfe Kerr]].<ref>{{citation|url= https://newsroom.churchofjesuschrist.org/article/elder-w.-rolfe-kerr-to-guide-church-educational-system|work=Newsroom|publisher=[[LDS Church]]|title=Elder W. Rolfe Kerr to Guide Church Educational System|date=14 January 2005}}</ref>

==LDS Church service==
[[File:Henry B. Eyring2.jpg|thumb|100px|left|Eyring while president of Ricks College]]
Among other callings in the LDS Church, Eyring has served as a [[Regional representative of the Twelve|regional representative]], [[Bishop (Latter Day Saints)|bishop]] and member of the [[Sunday School (LDS Church)|Sunday School General Board]].<ref name = ldsbio>{{citation |url= https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/church/leader/henry-b-eyring |title= President Henry B. Eyring |work= Organization: General Authorities |access-date= 2014-08-19 }}</ref> Eyring served as an early-morning seminary teacher early in his time as a professor at Stanford University, and as bishop of the Stanford singles ward later on.

Eyring served as president of [[Ricks College]] from 1971 to 1977, as a counselor to [[Presiding Bishop (LDS Church)|Presiding Bishop]] [[Robert D. Hales]] from 1985 to 1992, and as a member of the First Quorum of the Seventy, from 1992 to 1995.

Following the death of [[President of the Church (LDS Church)|church president]] [[Howard W. Hunter]], Eyring was sustained as a member of the church's Quorum of the Twelve Apostles on April 1, 1995 and ordained an apostle later that week.

Eyring was sustained as second counselor in the church's First Presidency on October 6, 2007,<ref>{{citation|url=https://newsroom.churchofjesuschrist.org/article/church-president-names-new-leaders|title=Church President Names New Leaders|work=Newsroom|date=7 October 2007|publisher=LDS Church}}</ref> filling the vacancy left by the August 10, 2007, death of [[James E. Faust]]. When the First Presidency was reorganized following the death of Gordon B. Hinckley, Eyring was called as the first counselor on February 3, 2008. The new First Presidency, with Monson as president, was announced on February 4, 2008.<ref>{{citation|url=https://newsroom.churchofjesuschrist.org/ldsnewsroom/eng/news-releases-stories/thomas-s-monson-named-16th-church-president|title=Thomas S. Monson Named 16th Church President|date=4 February 2008|work=Newsroom|publisher= LDS Church}} </ref>

Following Monson's death, Eyring was announced on January 16, 2018, as second counselor to Nelson, with Dallin H. Oaks as first counselor.<ref> {{citation|url=https://newsroom.churchofjesuschrist.org/article/russell-m-nelson-17th-church-president|title=Russell M. Nelson Named 17th Church President| date=18 January 2018|work=Newsroom|publisher= LDS Church}} </ref> After Nelson's death, Eyring was set apart as first counselor to Oaks in the First Presidency on October 14, 2025, with [[D. Todd Christofferson]] serving as second counselor.<ref>{{citation|url=https://newsroom.churchofjesuschrist.org/article/president-oaks-new-first-presidency|title=Dallin H. Oaks Named 18th Church President|date= 14 October 2025|work=Newsroom|publisher=LDS Church}}</ref> 

Following the death of [[Jeffrey R. Holland]] on December 27, 2025, Eyring became the most senior apostle behind church president Oaks and became president of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, with Dieter F. Uchtdorf being [[set apart]] as the quorum's acting president on January 8, 2026.<ref>{{citation|url=https://newsroom.churchofjesuschrist.org/article/dieter-f--uchtdorf--new-acting-president-of-the-quorum-of-the-twelve-apostles|title=Dieter F. Uchtdorf: New Acting President of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles|date=8 January 2026|work=Newsroom|publisher=LDS Church}}</ref>

https://newsroom.churchofjesuschrist.org/article/san-salvador-el-salvador-temple-dedication |title= San Salvador El Salvador Temple Dedicated |work= Newsroom |publisher= LDS Church |date= 2011-08-11 In 2014, after a meeting with [[Pope Francis]],<ref>{{cite magazine|url = http://www.nationalreview.com/article/393232/romes-extraordinary-ecumenical-event-maggie-gallagher|date = November 21, 2014|title = Rome's Extraordinary Ecumenical Event: What I and others learned from other faiths at a special event on the family|first = Maggie|last = Gallagher |author-link = Maggie Gallagher|magazine = [[National Review]]}}</ref><ref name = pope>{{cite news|url = http://www.sltrib.com/lifestyle/faith/1836619-155/eyring-marriage-pope-address-conference-environments|author-link = Peggy Fletcher Stack|first = Peggy Fletcher|last = Stack|date = November 17, 2014|newspaper = Salt Lake Tribune|title = Pope, Mormon leader make history with a handshake}}</ref> Eyring spoke at Humanum, "an International Interreligious Colloquium on The Complementarity of Man and Woman," held in [[Vatican City]].<ref>[https://newsroom.churchofjesuschrist.org/article/transcript-president-eyring-addresses-vatican-summit-marriage "Transcript: President Eyring Addresses the Vatican Summit on Marriage"]. ''Mormon Newsroom'', 18 November 2014.</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://humanum.it/en/program/ |title=Humanum &#124; Program |access-date=2014-11-19 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141119062334/http://humanum.it/en/program/ |archive-date=2014-11-19 }}</ref> It was the first time that a pope and a top LDS general authority ever met.<ref name = pope/>

==Personal life==
Eyring and his wife, Kathleen Johnson, met at a [[Single adult (LDS Church)|YSA]] meeting held at [[Rindge, New Hampshire]] at the [[Cathedral of the Pines]] in the spring of 1960. They became further acquainted at a meeting at the LDS Longfellow Park Chapel in Cambridge, Massachusetts, the next summer. Johnson was a native of Palo Alto and was a student at Stanford University. She had previously studied summers at the [[University of Vienna]] and [[University of Paris]] and was studying at Harvard University the summer she met Eyring. Wilbur Cox, the LDS Church's district president (to whom Eyring was serving as a counselor), made accommodations to facilitate Eyring's dating Johnson.<ref>Eaton and Eyring, ''I Will Lead You Along'', p. 89-90</ref> After an intense courtship that first summer, Eyring and Johnson continued courting with her making multiple cross-country airplane trips until they were engaged early in 1961.<ref>Eaton and Eyring, ''I Will Lead You Along'', p. 100</ref> They were married in the LDS Church's [[Logan Utah Temple|Logan Temple]] on July 27, 1962, with the ceremony performed by his uncle, Spencer W. Kimball.<ref>[[Robert D. Hales]], [https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/ensign/2008/07/president-henry-b-eyring-called-of-god?lang=eng "President Henry B. Eyring: Called of God"], [[Ensign (LDS magazine)|Ensign]], July 2008, pp.&nbsp;8–15.</ref> The couple were married for 61 years until Kathleen's death on October 15, 2023, at the age of 82.<ref>Ashley Fredde, [https://www.ksl.com/article/50753246/kathleen-eyring-wife-of-president-henry-b-eyring-dies-at-age-82 "Kathleen Eyring, wife of President B. Eyring, dies at age 82,"] KSL, Oct. 15, 2023.</ref>

They are the parents of six children (four sons and two daughters).<ref name = ldsbio/> Their sons include [[Henry J. Eyring]], past president of [[BYU–Idaho]] (2017 to 2023); and Matthew J. Eyring, the chief strategy innovation officer of [[Vivint]], a home automation company in North America. Eyring is a first cousin once-removed of former Michigan governor [[George W. Romney]]; his paternal grandmother was Romney's aunt. As of 2023, Eyring had 34 grandchildren and 31 great-grandchildren.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gibson |first=Rachel Sterzer |date=2023-10-21 |title=Sister Kathleen Johnson Eyring remembered as beloved wife, mother and ‘true woman of God’ |url=https://www.thechurchnews.com/leaders/2023/10/21/23926601/sister-kathleen-johnson-eyring-funeral-wife-president-henry-b-eyring/ |access-date=2026-05-24 |website=Church News |language=en}}</ref>
